Abstract
Most quantum computers today are constrained by hardware lim-
itations, particularly the number of available qubits, causing sig-
nificant challenges for executing large-scale quantum algorithms.
Circuit cutting has emerged as a key technique to overcome these
limitations by decomposing large quantum circuits into smaller sub-
circuits that can be executed independently and later reconstructed.
In this work, we introduce Qdislib, a distributed and flexible library
for quantum circuit cutting, designed to seamlessly integrate with
hybrid quantum-classical high-performance computing (HPC) sys-
tems. Qdislib employs a graph-based representation of quantum
circuits to enable efficient partitioning, manipulation and execu-
tion, supporting both wire cutting and gate cutting techniques. The
library is compatible with multiple quantum computing libraries,
including Qiskit and Qibo, and leverages distributed computing
frameworks to execute subcircuits across CPUs, GPUs, and quan-
tum processing units (QPUs) in a fully parallelized manner. We
present a proof of concept demonstrating how Qdislib enables
the distributed execution of quantum circuits across heterogeneous
computing resources, showcasing its potential for scalable quantum-
classical workflows.

Quantum Computing, High Performance Computing, Distributed
Computing, PyCOMPSs, Circuit Cutting
1
Introduction
As quantum computing (QC) matures, its integration into classical
high-performance computing (HPC) infrastructures has emerged
as a key strategy to unlock its potential for solving large-scale com-
putational problems. However, current quantum hardware remains
limited in scale and fidelity, constraining the execution of complex
quantum algorithms. In particular, today’s quantum processors sup-
port only a modest number of noisy qubits with short coherence
times, making it difficult to run circuits beyond a few tens of qubits
without approximation or decomposition strategies.
Circuit cutting has recently gained attention as a promising tech-
nique to bypass current hardware limitations by partitioning large
quantum circuits into smaller subcircuits. These subcircuits can
be executed independently—on either quantum or classical simu-
lators—and their results combined to reconstruct global outcomes.
This enables the execution of quantum algorithms beyond the phys-
ical qubit count of a single device and allows hybrid workflows to
be mapped to heterogeneous architectures.
In this work, we introduce Qdislib, an open-source, distributed
library designed for scalable quantum circuit cutting and execution
across hybrid HPC-QC systems. Qdislib leverages a graph-based
intermediate representation of quantum circuits to support both
wire and gate cutting strategies, and is compatible with popular
quantum software frameworks such as Qiskit and Qibo. Built on the
PyCOMPSs task-based programming model, Qdislib orchestrates
subcircuit execution across CPUs, GPUs, and quantum process-
ing units (QPUs), enabling fully parallel, hybrid quantum-classical
workflows.
We present a proof-of-concept deployment of Qdislib within a
supercomputing environment, demonstrating how circuit cutting
can facilitate the seamless integration of quantum backends—both
on-premise and cloud-based—into classical simulation pipelines.
The main contributions of this work are:
• The extension of distributed task-based environment to simulta-
neously control simulations in production CPU and GPU systems,
as well as on real quantum systems.
• A demonstration of the performance of Qdislib for representa-
tive quantum circuit-cutting applications, employing both CPU
and GPU environments, as well as a digital quantum computer
integrated into a supercomputer and a cloud-accessed quantum
computer. In doing so, we contributed to and validated the full in-
tegration of a hybrid quantum and high-performance computing
infrastructure.
2
Motivation and background
2.1
Quantum computing fundamentals
Quantum computing can be broadly divided into analog and digital
models, with this work focusing on the digital, gate-based para-
digm—the most widely adopted approach and closest comparison
to classical computing.

Quantum algorithms are implemented as sequences of quantum
gates acting on qubits, the fundamental units of quantum infor-
mation. A single qubit is described by a unit vector |𝜓⟩in a two-
dimensional complex Hilbert space. For 𝑛qubits, the global state
resides in a 2𝑛-dimensional Hilbert space. Quantum gates, repre-
sented by unitary matrices [22], evolve the system in a reversible
manner.
Simulating quantum circuits on classical hardware becomes ex-
ponentially expensive with increasing qubit count, due to the need
to store and manipulate 2𝑛-dimensional vectors. This exponential
scaling leads to the so-called quantum advantage regime, where
quantum devices outperform classical simulations. To delay this
barrier, various classical techniques and software tools have been
developed to improve simulation efficiency [23].
The computational power of quantum systems arises from their
ability to represent superpositions of many classical bit strings and
manipulate them via interference. Final measurements collapse the
quantum state to a classical outcome, and repeated runs produce
a probability distribution over bit strings. This distribution can be
used to estimate observable expectation values, such as ⟨ˆ𝐸⟩for a
Hermitian operator ˆ𝐸.
A central feature of quantum circuits is entanglement—non-
classical correlations between qubits that arise through multi-qubit
gate operations. Entanglement prevents decomposing a circuit
into independent parts without affecting the global quantum state.
Nonetheless, circuit cutting techniques allow for partitioning en-
tangled circuits into smaller components, at the cost of additional
computational overhead, as discussed in later sections.
2.2
Quantum circuit cutting
Current-term quantum computers have a limited number of qubits
per quantum processing unit (QPU) constrained by the techno-
logical developments of the physical platform. To scale quantum
computational capabilities, most platforms will likely rely on inter-
connecting multiple QPUs through quantum or classical channels.
Additionally, as quantum circuits increase in complexity (measured
by the number of qubits and gates), scalability becomes a critical
challenge. Circuit cutting has emerged as a promising technique
for partitioning large quantum circuits into smaller, more manage-
able subcircuits, preserving computational coherence while par-
tially mitigating scalability limitations. In this work, we focus on
two methods of circuit cutting – wire cutting [24, 27] and gate
cutting [20] – and assume classical communication between the
resulting subcircuits.

2.3
PyCOMPSs
PyCOMPSs [3, 30] is a task-based programming model and runtime
for parallel execution across heterogeneous computing resources
such as CPUs, GPUs, and distributed systems. It supports dynamic
task scheduling and automatic data dependency management, sim-
plifying the development of parallel applications without requiring
explicit control over resource allocation. PyCOMPSs has been ap-
plied in domains including biomedicine, engineering, chemistry,
astrophysics, and earth sciences [1, 7, 10, 13, 14, 18, 21].
While PyCOMPSs is not natively designed for quantum com-
puting or quantum processing units (QPUs), it has been used in
related contexts, such as parallelizing the RosneT library for dis-
tributed tensor algebra [25]. In this work, we extend its capabilities
through Qdislib, which introduces quantum-aware tasks and ab-
stracts QPU execution as a backend. This integration enables hybrid
quantum-classical workflows, where PyCOMPSs can schedule and
manage sub-circuits dynamically across CPUs, GPUs, and QPUs.
By combining PyCOMPSs with Qdislib, we enable efficient
parallel execution of circuit-cut subcircuits on the most suitable
hardware, optimizing resource utilization and reducing runtime
overhead in hybrid quantum-classical applications.
3
Qdislib Overview
Qdislib is a specialized Python library developed to perform scal-
able and modular quantum circuit cutting. It was designed specif-
ically to address the limitations of current quantum hardware by
enabling the decomposition and distributed execution of large quan-
tum circuits on hybrid classical-quantum infrastructures. At its
core, Qdislib provides the full circuit cutting pipeline—from graph-
based circuit representation to subcircuit generation, execution on
various backends (CPU, GPU, or QPU), and result reconstruction.
The orchestration layer, implemented using PyCOMPSs [30], only
handles task scheduling and distributed execution, while all domain-
specific logic, optimizations, and quantum-classical interfaces are
fully implemented within Qdislib.
Qdislib was developed from the ground up with extensibility
and backend-agnosticism in mind. It supports multiple quantum
programming frameworks, including Qiskit [16] and Qibo [12],
and can interoperate with both classical HPC simulators and real
quantum devices—local or cloud-based. The library includes ded-
icated interfaces for interacting with simulators (e.g., Qiskit Aer,
Qibo backends), IBM Quantum cloud services, and custom quantum
execution pipelines.
3.1
Graph-Based Circuit Representation and
Transformation
A key point of Qdislib is its use of a graph-based internal represen-
tation to model quantum circuits. When a user submits a quantum
circuit, Qdislib first translates it into a Directed Acyclic Graph
(DAG), where nodes correspond to quantum gates and edges rep-
resent their temporal and causal dependencies. This abstraction
enables efficient and scalable manipulation of circuit structure and
allows the implementation of cutting strategies to remain indepen-
dent of the quantum programming language used.
All cut-related operations—including wire and gate cuts, DAG
rewriting, measurement insertion, and circuit splitting—are imple-
mented directly within Qdislib. This includes support for detecting
and transforming gates that need to be decomposed during gate
cutting, and mechanisms for inserting intermediate measurements
and classical post-processing instructions as required.
The framework ensures language compatibility by performing
automatic translations between quantum circuit representations if
the original language lacks necessary features (e.g., intermediate
measurement support). For instance, a Qiskit circuit may be con-
verted to Qibo for execution if the target backend requires it. All
such conversions and validation are handled internally by Qdislib,
preserving correctness and reproducibility.
3.2
Wire and Gate Cutting Implementation
Qdislib supports both wire and gate cutting approaches using
highly configurable and modular workflows. After converting the
original circuit into its DAG form, users can either manually define
cut locations or rely on an automated FindCut function included in
the library, which analyzes circuit structure and suggests candidate
cuts based on graph properties and user-specified criteria.
• Wire Cutting involves selecting edges between pairs of
gates on the same qubit to sever the quantum correlations,
resulting in 8𝑘possible subcircuit combinations for 𝑘cuts.
• Gate Cutting involves the decomposition of specific two-
qubit gates (e.g., CZ, CNOT) into combinations of single-
qubit operations and classical post-processing, yielding 6𝑘
combinations.
Qdislib fully automates the decomposition of gates for the
gate-cutting case, including the insertion of projective measure-
ments, classical conditioning, and stochastic sampling following
quasi-probability decomposition techniques [20]. For both cutting

3.3
Subcircuit Execution and Parallelism
While PyCOMPSs is used to orchestrate the execution workflow—
including subcircuit simulation, and result aggregation— all quan-
tum logic, data structures, and runtime logic are handled exclusively
by Qdislib. PyCOMPSs is invoked only to parallelize the execution
across multicore CPUs or distributed HPC environments and does
not contribute to any algorithmic or structural transformation of
the quantum circuits. Each subcircuit is scheduled independently
by PyCOMPSs, which triggers calls to the corresponding simulator
or hardware backend via the Qdislib execution interface.
3.4
Result Aggregation and Reconstruction
Once all subcircuits are executed, Qdislib performs result aggre-
gation and reconstruction using built-in implementations of the
quasi-probability and wire-cutting reconstruction formulas [24].
Users can tune sampling precision, choose between exact or ap-
proximate reconstructions depending on the simulator, and analyze
statistical error margins. These reconstruction routines are imple-
mented directly in Qdislib and are compatible with output formats
from both simulators and hardware backends.
Importantly, Qdislib ensures that the reconstructed expecta-
tion values match those of the original (uncut) circuit up to the
statistical precision dictated by the number of shots and sampling
configuration.
4
Evaluation
This section presents the benchmarking methodology used to eval-
uate the performance of Qdislib for large-scale quantum circuit
execution via circuit cutting. We focus on assessing its scalability,
resource orchestration, and hybrid quantum-classical integration.
Qdislib supports both wire and gate cutting; however, our eval-
uation focuses on gate cutting, which is more efficient for most
applications due to common qubit connectivity patterns that favor
fewer and simpler cuts.
We benchmark Qdislib using two representative families:
• Hardware-Efficient Ansatz (HEA): A widely used NISQ-
era circuit design that balances depth and connectivity con-
straints [6]. It is representative of workloads such as the
Quantum Fourier Transform, graph states, or variational
algorithms.
• Random Quantum Circuits (RQC): Inspired by Google’s
quantum supremacy experiments [2], these circuits feature
complex entanglement and high depth, similar to workloads
in quantum simulation and benchmarking.
For both benchmarks, gates are initialized with random angles,
and we compute the expectation value of the observable 𝑍⊗𝑛, where
𝑛is the number of qubits in the full circuit.
Computational backends:
We consider four types of computational backends—CPUs, GPUs,
local QPUs, and cloud QPUs—used individually or in hybrid com-
binations. Classical backends include general-purpose CPUs and
NVIDIA GPUs. Quantum executions use digital superconducting
QPUs, accessed both locally (via BSC infrastructure) and remotely
(via IBMQ Cloud).
4.1
Execution infrastructure
Experiments were conducted on MareNostrum 5, a EuroHPC pre-
exascale supercomputer with three partitions:
• GPP (General-Purpose): 6,408 nodes with 2× Intel Xeon
Platinum 8480 CPUs (112 cores at 2GHz).
• ACC (Accelerated): 1,120 nodes, each with 2× Intel Xeon
8460Y+ CPUs (80 cores) and 4× NVIDIA H100 GPUs.
• ONA (Quantum): A 5-qubit superconducting QPU oper-
ated as part of MareNostrum Ona, arranged in a star topol-
ogy. Future upgrades target up to 35 qubits.
All partitions share a common GPFS file system. GPP and ACC
share a single Slurm instance, while Ona uses a separate sched-
uler (a federated instance is planned). Quantum programming uses
Qibo [12] (gate-level) and Qililab [29] (pulse-level), with Qibo code
compiled into Qililab format for execution.
For cloud-based QPU access, we use IBM Quantum’s IBMQ-
Marrakesh, a 156-qubit superconducting processor with heavy-hex
connectivity [28], accessed via the Qiskit framework [16].
4.2
Execution environment
Our hybrid execution spans distributed CPUs, GPUs, and QPUs
with distinct architectures and service models (on-premise clusters

As illustrated in Figure 4, execution begins with submitting a
quantum circuit using the PyCOMPSs CLI. A Slurm job on GPP or
ACC partitions performs the circuit cutting, generating subcircuits
and dispatching them based on the target backend (CPU, GPU,
QPU).
GPP and ACC resources can be used jointly within a single job.
Ona, however, requires a persistent agent listening for execution
requests. Communication occurs via the shared GPFS filesystem
using file-based signaling between the job and the agent.
For IBM Quantum Cloud, integration is more complex due to
external network restrictions in MareNostrum 5. To address this,
QPU Cloud tasks are routed via CPU nodes to the user’s laptop
using port forwarding. A local proxy then communicates with the
IBM Cloud API, enabling remote QPU execution. These integration
mechanisms enable seamless orchestration of all backends, support-
ing efficient hybrid execution across heterogeneous infrastructures.
Classical simulations are performed using the Qiskit-Aer sim-
ulator [16] for CPU-based, full wavefunction execution, and the
cuStateVec simulator from NVIDIA’s cuQuantum framework [4]
for GPU-accelerated runs. All simulations use 1024 shots to ensure
consistent results across different hardware backends.
4.3
Benchmark 1: Hardware Efficient Ansatz
The first benchmark consists of cutting a quantum circuit with
a Hardware-Efficient structure (Hardware-Efficient ansatz (HEA)).
The quantum computing community employs this particular circuit
architecture to design parameterized quantum circuits leveraging
state-of-the-art hardware capabilities. There are many proposed
HEA designs, all of them sharing a layered structure: each layer
is composed of single-qubit gates applied to all qubits in parallel,
followed by two-qubit gates that entangle the qubits in a ladder-like
pattern. This layer is applied 𝐿times, increasing the quantum cir-
cuit’s depth and complexity. In particular, we use the HEA obtained
from the he_circuit function from Qibo [12] that employs single-
qubit rotational gates and CZ two-qubit gates. The total circuit
depth scales linearly with the number of qubits 𝑛and the number
of layers 𝐿, following the expression (2 + 𝑛)𝐿. When the circuit is
partitioned into multiple subcircuits, each subcircuit retains the
same linear depth scaling, (2 + 𝑚)𝐿, where 𝑚is the number of
qubits of the subcircuit.

Figure 7: Execution time for HEA circuits varying cuts.
Figure 7 compares simulation times when applying 4, 5, and 6
cuts to circuits of 32 and 96 qubits (left and right plots, respectively).
In both cases, the number of fragments and their size depend on the
number of cuts. For the 32-qubit circuit, 4 cuts yield 4 subcircuits of
8 qubits; 5 cuts result in two subcircuits of 7 qubits and 3 of 6 qubits;
and 6 cuts produce two subcircuits of 6 qubits and 4 of 5 qubits. The
left plot shows that increasing the number of cuts in this smaller
circuit introduces considerable overhead, leading to longer simula-
tion times—especially in the 6-cut case—and reduced scalability as
more nodes are added. This is because the benefit of smaller subcir-
cuits is outweighed by the cost of managing more fragments and
performing the reconstruction. On the other hand, the right plot,
corresponding to the 96-qubit circuit, shows the opposite trend: the
configuration with 6 cuts (producing two subcircuits of 26 qubits
and four of 25) outperforms the others. Even a 1-2 qubit reduction
per fragment significantly improves performance for larger circuits,
where simulation cost grows exponentially with qubit count. This
highlights a crucial insight: the optimal number of cuts depends
heavily on circuit size and properties. While additional cuts may
degrade performance in small circuits, they can greatly improve
efficiency in large-scale simulations.

Benchmark 2: Random Circuits
For the second benchmark, we use the Google quantum supremacy
circuit [2]. Our goal is to asses the Qdislib using a highly con-
nected quantum circuit that also has remarkable applications in
demonstrating the computational advantage of quantum computers.
In the original quantum circuit, the entangling gates employed are
the fermionic simulation gates (𝑓𝑆𝑖𝑚). Since the focus of this work
is to test the optimal cutting scheme and evaluate the computational
scaling, we simplify the circuits used by replacing the original 𝑓𝑆𝑖𝑚
gates with CZ gates, whose gate-cutting protocol is simpler. Be-
cause we do not use the 𝑓𝑆𝑖𝑚gate, we refer to the resulting circuits
as Random circuits (RC). However, the same benchmark could be
executed by either finding an optimal gate-cutting protocol for the
𝑓𝑆𝑖𝑚gate or by decomposing it into CZ and single-qubit gates. The
connectivity of the simulated circuit is shown in Figure 9 (left).

Related Work
Circuit cutting is a technique for decomposing large quantum cir-
cuits into smaller, independently executable fragments, which are
later reconstructed to approximate the original circuit’s output.
This strategy is particularly useful in overcoming memory and run-
time limitations when simulating large-scale quantum circuits. Our
work builds upon the circuit cutting methods introduced in [20, 24],
which lay the foundation for both simulation and hardware execu-
tion scenarios.
Additional contributions have expanded the scope of circuit
cutting. For wire cutting, notable works include [9, 11, 19, 27],
while gate cutting approaches are explored in [5, 15, 31]. Some of
these efforts also connect circuit cutting to applications in quantum
communication and optimization of quantum resources.
In distributed quantum computing, FitCut [17] presents a Qiskit-
based framework for executing cut circuits across multi-node quan-
tum systems. It introduces a static scheduling algorithm to opti-
mize task placement, whereas our work leverages the dynamic
scheduling capabilities of PyCOMPSs. Extending PyCOMPSs with
quantum-aware scheduling policies for multi-node QPU systems
remains a promising direction for future research.


Mar Tejedor, Berta Casas, Javier Conejero, Alba Cervera-Lierta, and Rosa M. Badia
Other efforts, such as ATLAS [32], have explored large-scale
quantum circuit simulation on multi-GPU systems. Their method
partitions circuits into simulation stages to minimize inter-node
communication, demonstrating scalability up to 256 GPUs using
FlexFlow and Legion. In contrast, our approach uses traditional cir-
cuit cutting and supports heterogeneous backends—including CPUs,
GPUs, local QPUs, cloud QPUs, and hybrid execution—offering
broader applicability beyond GPU-based simulation.
CutQC [27] also applies circuit cutting to simulate large quantum
circuits on smaller devices. Although it includes a parallel recon-
struction phase, its scalability is limited to 16 nodes with low-core
CPUs, and the implementation lacks detail. While CutQC was once
integrated into the Qiskit circuit cutting addon, it has been dep-
recated since version 0.9.0. In this work, we also compare against
IBM’s Qiskit circuit cutting addon [8], which provides a baseline
for evaluation.
6
Conclusions
In this work, we presented Qdislib, a high-performance, distributed
quantum library designed for hybrid HPC-quantum executions. We
used quantum circuit cutting as the first feature of this library
leveraging its applications in quantum algorithms scalability and
its parallelizable nature. We tested the performance of Qdislib
by employing two representative benchmarks - HEA and Random
Circuits - for quantum computing applications. We execute these
benchmarks in a highly hybrid environment composed by CPUs,
GPUs and QPUs, accessed both locally and through the cloud. We
demonstrate efficient scalability when executing on CPU and GPU,
as well as the efficiency of an hybrid quantum-classical execution.
The graph-based representation of quantum circuits used at
the core of Qdislib, together with the open-source task-based
programming model PyCOMPSs used to orchestrate the executions,
makes this tool flexible and hardware-agnostic.
Quantum computers are still too small and prone to errors to
test most real-world applications and thus, circuit cutting is useful
both in the short and long term. In this context, quantum emulation
(quantum simulation in classical devices) has emerged as a near-
term solution by simulating quantum applications in a noise-free
environment using traditional computation. Even though emula-
tion is limited to a few qubits in general, the quantum advantage
frontier can be extended in favor of classical computation if these
resources are managed properly. Qdislib demonstrates how this
task can be made efficient, as shown in the almost ideal speed-up
of the executions in CPU and GPU. Moreover, while this work used
two standard quantum simulators, Qdislib is modular and can be
extended to incorporate other backends. For example, simulators
based on Tensor Networks [23] are highly parallelizable as was
shown in [25], also based in PyCOMPSs, making it natural to merge
it with Qdislib in future research.
Other improvements in Qdislib are possible by exploring reduc-
tions in the number of subcircuits needed for each cut. Although
the scaling remains exponential with the number of cuts, certain op-
timization strategies can be adopted, depending on the structure of
the circuits [26] or the measurement technique applied [19]. Finally,
Qdislib can be extended to other quantum computing applications
beyond circuit cutting such as variational quantum algorithms or
quantum error correction, both of which require an efficient man-
agement of quantum and classical computing resources.
In summary, we developed an open-source1, flexible, hardware-
agnostic, and distributed High-Performance quantum library that
can execute quantum algorithms in hybrid computational environ-
ments. With Qdislib’s benchmarks on real quantum and HPC in-
frastructures, wendemonstrated full quantum-classical integration
and contributed to extending the capabilities of high-performance
computing.

Abstract: Most quantum computers today are constrained by hardware lim- itations, particularly the number of available qubits, causing sig- nificant challenges for executing large-scale quantum algorithms. Circuit cutting has emerged as a key technique to overcome these limitations by decomposing large quantum circuits into smaller sub- circuits that can be executed independently and later reconstructed. In this work, we introduce Qdislib, a distributed and flexible library for quantum circuit cutting, designed to seamlessly integrate with hybrid quantum-classical high-performance computing (HPC) sys- tems. Qdislib employs a graph-based representation of quantum circuits to enable efficient partitioning, manipulation and execu- tion, supporting both wire cutting and gate cutting techniques. The library is compatible with multiple quantum computing libraries, including Qiskit and Qibo, and leverages distributed computing frameworks to execute subcircuits across CPUs, GPUs, and quan- tum processing units (QPUs) in a fully parallelized manner. We present a proof of concept demonstrating how Qdislib enables the distributed execution of quantum circuits across heterogeneous computing resources, showcasing its potential for scalable quantum- classical workflows.
